--- Page 1 ---
Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial
Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
Ruike Lyu and Bolun Xu
Columbia University, Earth and Environmental Engineering, New York, NY, USA
Email: rl3763@columbia.edu, bx2177@columbia.edu
Abstract—We show that co-locating distributed AI servers
with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with
production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid
interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection
is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data
centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their
peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during
production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes
CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and
routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-
site architectures with new large data centers serving the same
demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing
industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do
not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and
scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less
additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers,
and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group’s factories.
Index Terms—AI computing load, data center flexibility, grid
interconnection, industrial load, workload scheduling
I. INTRODUCTION
Rapid growth in AI computing load is driving up global
data-center electricity use and interconnection needs [1]. Be-
cause new generation and grid infrastructure take years to
plan, permit, and build, large data centers can face lengthy
interconnection delays [2]. Efforts to ease this bottleneck focus
on expanding the electricity infrastructure available to data
centers and making data-center demand more flexible [3].
Shifting data-center workloads across time and locations has
long been studied as a way to reduce electricity costs, emis-
sions, and peak demand charges [4]. More recently, such
flexibility has been examined as a means of accelerating large-
load interconnection and reducing the grid capacity that new
data centers require [5], [6]. These measures make it easier to
integrate large data centers into the grid, but the AI computing
load is still located at new sites, each of which needs its own
grid connection.
With the growing capability and hardware efficiency of
open-weight models [7], [8], deploying local AI servers at
factory sites offers a promising alternative to meet part of en-
terprises’ own AI needs. Factory grid connections are sized for
peak production loads, which provides considerable intercon-
nection headroom during non-peak use times [9]. AI servers
placed at factories can use this spare capacity depending on
the type of AI services and when these tasks run. Interactive
This work was partly supported by the National Science Foundation under
award ECCS-2239046 and by Columbia School of Engineering and Applied
Science Interdisciplinary Research Seed Funding.
services such as office assistants must respond immediately,
but tasks such as R&D simulation and production scheduling
can often wait for hours and run when production loads are
low. Factory-site deployment therefore has the potential to
reduce the additional interconnection capacity needed for AI
loads.
This study quantifies the additional grid-interconnection
capacity required by AI computing loads when they are
deployed at factory sites and coordinated with production
loads. It addresses a gap in the literature where commercial
investment has concentrated on hyperscalers and ever-larger
AI models, while the potential of efficient open-weight models
running on local AI servers to meet industrial AI demand more
cost-effectively and sustainably has been largely overlooked.
The contributions of this paper are as follows.
• We formulate a sizing-and-scheduling model to jointly
determine server size and AI task schedules around pro-
duction loads, and use it to study various AI deployment
architectures.
• Using projected 2030 AI demand and measured hourly
production loads for 31 Chinese manufacturing indus-
tries [10], we compare three factory-site architectures and
benchmark them with centralized data center solutions.
• Our study shows that new large data centers would re-
quire 1,488 MW of additional interconnection capacity to
serve the studied industrial AI demand, whereas factory-
site deployment would require 556–576 MW, or as little
as 30 MW with routing among factories. Most individual
factory sites require less than 1 MW.
We formulate the problem in Section II, and present the case
study in Section III. Section IV concludes the paper.
II. PROBLEM AND MODEL
A. Service Scope and Deployment Architectures
We consider scenarios in which manufacturers use AI
services for their own operations, which can run either on-site
or in a shared computing pool. These AI services are solely
for manufacturer business support. We classify these AI de-
mands into six categories: office knowledge services, business-
process agents, visual quality review, predictive maintenance
and diagnosis, production scheduling and optimization, and
R&D simulations & digital twins. Large language models and
other foundation models are integral to many of these services,
typically interpreting requests and orchestrating workflows.
arXiv:2611.18951v1  [cs.DC]  13 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---

Host-factory (HFD)

Fig. 1. Illustration of the four AI server deployment architectures.
Specialized models, optimizers, and simulators perform the
majority of underlying CPU and GPU computations. Demand
for each class is categorized as either firm demand, which must
be served immediately upon arrival, or flexible demand, which
can be delayed until an intraday or multi-day (batch) deadline.
Service is quantified in reference workload units, and server
throughput in such units per server-hour.
We consider four AI server deployment architectures
(Fig. 1). Per-factory deployment (PFD) runs each service
locally at its source factory. Host-factory deployment (HFD)
runs all services for a corporate group at a single designated
factory site. Multi-site deployment (MSD) allows tasks to
be routed among several factories in the group within their
deadlines. Large-data-center deployment (LDC) serves the
same AI demand in new facilities without existing load or grid
connections. Both HFD and LDC consolidate computing at a
single site; however, HFD utilizes the existing grid connection
of a host factory, where production load leaves part of the
connection capacity unused outside peak periods. In contrast,
LDC requires a new connection sized for its full AI load peak.
Each factory that hosts servers is defined as a computing node,
its AI load sharing the grid connection with the production
load.
B. Server Sizing and Scheduling Model
For each architecture a and industry, the enterprise de-
termines the sizing of CPU and GPU servers at each node
and schedules AI tasks over a representative horizon T to
minimize annualized cost. In the initial quantification, the
model is deterministic and assumes production loads Ln,t
are fixed. Therefore, any cost reduction results solely from
the placement and scheduling of the AI load, rather than
from industrial demand flexibility [12]. The nomenclature and
problem formulation are listed below.
Indices and sets:
a
Deployment architecture (PFD, HFD, MSD,
or LDC).
Na, n
Computing nodes under a; node.
h
Hardware type, CPU or GPU.
k
Task class.
j
Flexible job, with task class kj.
T , t
Hours of the representative horizon; hour.
Tj
Hours in which job j can be executed.
Decision variables:
zn,h
Installed server groups (integer).
vn,h,t
Online server groups.
un,h,t
Compute demand.
yk,n,t, xj,n,t
Executed firm and flexible service.
pn,t
AI load (facility power).
δn
Incremental connection capacity.

where each constraint holds for all indices that appear in it.
Objective: Equation (1a) defines the objective as the sum
of the annualized cost Ch for each installed server group,
the maximum-demand charge Cd for incremental connection
capacity, and the energy cost of the AI load at hourly prices
Πt, with the planning horizon repeated Y = 365/7 times per
year.
Service: Constraint (1b) requires that all firm service Rk,t
of task class k be executed in its arrival hour, with yk,n,t
denoting the portion executed at node n. Flexible demand
sharing the same task class, release hour Aj, and maximum
delay Fj is aggregated into a flexible job j. Constraint (1c)
ensures that each job’s volume Dj is completed within Tj =
{(Aj + τ) mod |T | : τ = 0, . . . , Fj}, where xj,n,t represents
the service of job j executed at node n in hour t, and xj,n,t = 0
for t /∈Tj.
Spatial allocation: In per-factory and host-factory deploy-
ments, the execution location of each service is predetermined,
resulting in each node executing a fixed share Ωn of every
firm task-hour and every flexible job (1d). In contrast, multi-
site deployment removes this constraint, allowing the time and
location of each task to be determined jointly.
Server sizing: The executed service generates compute
demand un,h,t on hardware h ∈{cpu, gpu} (1e), where Wk
denotes the compute required per unit of service and Qk,h
the compute routed to h per unit. Each online server group
vn,h,t can serve up to Gh per hour and cannot exceed the
number of installed server groups zn,h (1f), which constitutes
the sizing decision. Constraint (1i) sizes installed capacity at
least a planning margin r above average compute demand.
AI load and connection capacity: Each server group con-
sumes standby power Bh when installed and Ih when online
but idle, with power consumption increasing linearly to Ph
at full load. The facility-power multiplier Ma accounts for

Kn plus incremental capacity δn. Here, Kn = maxt Ln,t

is conservative since actual connections often have spare
contract or network capacity. Given Cd > 0, the optimal

demand due to AI, and the national requirement is P
n δn. For
new large data centers, Ln,t = 0 and Kn = 0, so the entire
AI peak is additional. The model can therefore avoid δn by
shifting or routing work away from production peaks, at the
cost of more servers or higher-priced energy hours.

the large-data-center deployment, the demand from all 31
industries is aggregated at a single node. This pooling is based
on average demand and is therefore conservative.
III. CASE STUDY
We consider a 2030 AI demand scenario estimated bottom-
up for 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, based on enter-
prise adoption, task coverage, and service intensity, consistent
with a reported national adoption rate above 30% [13]. In the
core scenario, demand reaches 96 million service units per day
(Fig. 2), or approximately 12 TWh/yr of AI facility electricity
in the model, representing about 0.25% of the projected

with firm shares of 10% and 25%, respectively. In contrast,

IV. RESULTS
A. Grid-Interconnection Requirements
All three factory-site architectures require substantially less
additional grid-interconnection capacity compared to new
large data centers serving equivalent AI demand (Table II).
National totals are 556 MW for per-factory deployment and
576 MW for host-factory deployment, representing reductions
of 63% and 61%, respectively, relative to the 1,488 MW
required by new large data centers. Multi-site deployment
1https://github.com/ruikelyu/distributed_LLM
further reduces the requirement to 30 MW, which is 98% lower
than that of new large data centers.
Factory-site deployment also requires much less capacity
at each connection point. In per-factory deployment, 68% of
sites require less than 0.1 MW of additional capacity, while
58% of host-factory sites require between 0.1 and 1 MW. In
multi-site deployment, more than 99% of sites require less than
0.1 MW, and 22% require no additional capacity (Fig. 3). For
comparison, 69 AI data centers and campuses in the Epoch AI
database [16], primarily located in the United States, exhibit
peak demands ranging from 21 to 1,135 MW, with a median
of 182 MW. Consequently, a new AI data center typically
requires a connection more than two orders of magnitude
larger than that required by a factory site.
B. Mechanisms of Capacity Reduction
Here we examine why co-locating AI computing with
production loads can reduce required network capacity.
1) Non-coincident AI and production peaks: Factory grid
connections are designed to accommodate production peaks,
resulting in unused connection capacity during off-peak pe-
riods that can be utilized to host AI servers (Fig. 4a,b). In
the absence of production loads at host sites, the entire AI
peak constitutes an additional demand, requiring 1,585 MW
for host-factory deployment, which is marginally higher than
the requirement for new large data centers due to a higher
facility multiplier. Co-location reduces this to 576 MW (64%).


--- Page 5 ---
Without task shifting (Fj = 0), the standalone requirement
is 2,372 MW, and co-location still reduces it to 1,343 MW
(43%), as AI and production peaks do not fully overlap.
2) Non-coincident peaks across factories: Factories en-
counter production peaks at different times, leading to variable
spare connection capacity across sites throughout the day.
Routing computing tasks to sites with available capacity
enables more efficient utilization of existing infrastructure
(Fig. 4c,d). If tasks remain fixed to their origin nodes as de-
fined in (1d), national multi-site deployment requires 562 MW.
Permitting routing among these nodes reduces the require-
ment to 30 MW, representing a 95% reduction. This analysis
assumes unrestricted routing of all tasks, without network
or data-residency limitations; therefore, the 95% reduction
illustrates the upper-bound benefit of cross-site routing.
C. Possible Infrastructure Reductions
Most factory sites require less than 1 MW of additional
network capacity, thereby avoiding the large-load intercon-
nection processes encountered by new AI data centers [2].
These additional peaks can also be shaved with batteries that
factories install and operate behind the meter [17]. We consider
one battery sized at each AI host site to cover its largest
daily excess above the pre-AI peak (only 1.6% of per-factory
sites, where AI load stays above the pre-AI peak for most
of the week, cannot fully shave the peak increase), based
on Chinese battery power and energy costs [14], [18]. For
multi-site deployment, batteries cost CNY 0.05 billion or less
(Table II). In comparison, the 220-kV substation and lines of
a 300-MVA data center in Datong cost CNY 0.23 billion [19],
or CNY 1.2 billion when scaled to 1,488 MW.
Factory-site deployment further reduces other infrastructure
requirements. Per-factory deployment uses 0.47 million m3
nationally of on-site cooling and humidification water per
year, about 85% less than new large data centers providing
equivalent service, because air-cooled factory server rooms are
assumed to use 0.05 L/kWh of IT energy, compared to about
0.33 L/kWh reported for air-cooled large data centers [20].
Per-factory deployment requires 0.92 million m2 of floor area,
or about 120 m2 per site, which can likely be accommodated
within existing industrial sites. In contrast, new large data cen-
ters require 1.34 million m2 of floor area and 0.38 million m2
of land conversion, estimated from public project filings [14].
These reductions need not increase enterprise payments, which
at public prices (Aug. 2026) are CNY 55 billion per year at
factory sites and CNY 95–101 billion for equivalent cloud
procurement.
V. CONCLUSION
We show that locating AI servers at factory sites reduces
the additional interconnection capacity needed to serve man-
ufacturers’ AI demand by 60% compared to building new
large data centers, and by up to 98% when AI tasks can
be routed among deployed servers across multiple factories
under the same enterprise. This is because AI and production
loads do not peak simultaneously, and flexible AI tasks can be
scheduled outside production peak periods. In addition, since
factories’ production loads peak at different times, AI tasks
can be assigned in real time to sites with network headroom,
further reducing needed interconnection capacity.
Beyond grid interconnection capacity, deploying distributed
AI servers could also reduce land and water use compared with
large data centers. Future research should further examine how
differences in computing capability and efficiency between
distributed and centralized architectures, temporal variations
and uncertainties in industrial production and AI demand affect
the achievable infrastructure savings and benefits of distributed
AI computing.
